title: Constitution of Alloys and Alloy Solidification

questions.text: A *solid solution* specifically:

options.label: a
options.text: consists of two types of atoms combined in **one** type of crystal structure in the solid state

options.label: b
options.text: has metallic properties and is composed of two or more chemical species, having at least one metal

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Solid solution = **one** crystal structure, single phase. Item (b) describes an *alloy* (broader). This was your Quiz I Q11 — learn the "one structure vs metal+other" test.
questions.concise: Solid solution = exactly **one** crystal structure, single phase. Alloy = broader.
questions.detailed:
**This is your Quiz I Q11.** The precise definitions:
- **Solid solution** — a single *liquid* phase solidifies into a single *solid* phase; the solute
  atoms sit inside the solvent's **one** type of crystal structure, throughout the alloy.
  The defining test: *does it have exactly one crystal structure?*
- **Alloy** — the umbrella term: any metallic combination of two or more chemical species (at
  least one metal), which *may* be single- or multi-phase and *may* include intermetallic
  compounds and mechanical mixtures.

- (b) describes an **alloy** (broader) — the trap in the original quiz.
- (c) false — a solid solution does not require an intermetallic compound.
- (d) false — a solid solution is by definition **single-phase**.

**The one-line test to memorise:** *solid solution = exactly one crystal structure; alloy = metal
+ other, any number of phases.* This distinction is worth more marks than any other single
definition in Chapter 4.

questions.text: Which statement(s) correctly distinguish an *alloy* from a *solid solution*?

statements.text: "Alloy" is the umbrella term — any metallic combination, single- or multi-phase.
"Solid solution" is the narrower case: solute atoms sit inside the solvent's one crystal structure, single phase throughout.
An alloy may include intermetallic compounds and mechanical mixtures.
Every alloy is by definition a solid solution.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 inverts the relationship (not every alloy is a solid solution).
questions.concise: Alloy is the umbrella term; solid solution is the narrower single-structure case; not every alloy is a solid solution.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: "alloy" is the umbrella term — any metallic combination, single- or multi-phase.
- Item 2 — TRUE: "solid solution" is the narrower case — solute atoms inside the solvent's *one*
  crystal structure, single phase throughout.
- Item 3 — TRUE: an alloy may also include intermetallic compounds and mechanical mixtures.
- Item 4 — FALSE: this *inverts* the relationship. Not every alloy is a solid solution — a
  two-phase alloy containing an intermetallic compound is an alloy but not a solid solution.
Item 4 is the false member. The relationship is one of *containment*: all solid solutions are
alloys, but not all alloys are solid solutions.

questions.text: In a *substitutional* solid solution, the solute atoms:

options.label: a
options.text: replace solvent atoms at normal lattice sites

options.label: b
options.text: sit in the gaps between solvent atoms

questions.keyExplanation: Substitutional = replace solvent atoms at lattice sites.
questions.concise: Substitutional = solute replaces solvent atoms at lattice sites.
questions.detailed:
In a **substitutional** solid solution the solute atoms occupy *normal lattice
sites*, replacing solvent atoms. The classic example is Cu–Ni (isomorphous, complete solubility).
- (b) describes an *interstitial* solid solution (Q4).
- (c) a separate phase would make it a two-phase alloy, not a solid solution.
- (d) segregation to grain boundaries is not what defines the structure.

questions.text: In an *interstitial* solid solution, the solute atoms:

options.label: b
options.text: occupy the interstices (gaps) between solvent atoms — e.g. C, N, H, B in iron

options.label: d
options.text: are always larger than the solvent atoms

questions.keyExplanation: Interstitial = occupy gaps; C/N/H/B in Fe is the classic case.
questions.concise: Interstitial = small atoms (C, N, H, B) in the gaps.
questions.detailed:
In an **interstitial** solid solution the solute atoms are *small enough* to sit in
the interstices (voids) between the larger solvent atoms. Only small non-metals qualify —
**carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen and boron** in iron — with carbon in iron being the classic and most
important metallurgical example.
- (a) describes a substitutional solution.
- (c) forming compounds is not required.
- (d) false — interstitial solutes are *smaller* than the host atoms (indeed smaller than the voids, though still usually larger than the void — see Q5).

questions.text: Which statement(s) about interstitial solid solutions is/are correct?

statements.text: Only small atoms (C, N, H, B) can occupy interstitial sites.
Carbon in iron is the classic and most important metallurgical example.
The solute is always smaller than the void it occupies, so no strain is created.
Interstitial solutes produce large, asymmetric lattice strain fields.

questions.keyExplanation: Item 3 is false — interstitial solutes *always* cost strain energy (C = 0.08 nm exceeds every void).
questions.concise: Only small atoms fit; C in Fe is the classic example; interstitials create large asymmetric strains — never "no strain".
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: only small atoms (C, N, H, B) can occupy interstitial sites.
- Item 2 — TRUE: carbon in iron is the classic and most important metallurgical example.
- Item 3 — FALSE: the solute is **not** always smaller than the void. Carbon (0.08 nm) is in fact
  *larger* than every available void in iron (Ch. 2 Q43), so dissolving it **always** costs
  lattice strain energy.
- Item 4 — TRUE: interstitial solutes produce large, asymmetric lattice strain fields.
Item 3 is the false member, and it is a *reversal* of the true state of affairs. That strain
energy is precisely why interstitials are such potent strengtheners (Ch. 7).

questions.text: The four Hume-Rothery factors governing substitutional solid solubility are:

statements.text: crystal structure factor
relative size factor
chemical affinity factor
relative valence factor

questions.keyExplanation: All four are the Hume-Rothery factors.
questions.concise: All four are Hume-Rothery factors: crystal structure, size, chemical affinity, valence.
questions.detailed:
The four empirical Hume-Rothery factors governing substitutional solid solubility:
1. **Crystal structure factor** — complete solubility only if both metals share the same structure.
2. **Relative size factor** — favoured when radii differ by less than ~15%.
3. **Chemical affinity factor** — stronger affinity restricts solubility.
4. **Relative valence factor** — a lower-valence metal dissolves more of a higher-valence one.

All four are genuine, so this is an "all are correct" case. Memorising the four *names* lets you
answer any "which of the following is a Hume-Rothery rule?" question instantly.

questions.text: Complete (total) solid solubility across the whole composition range is only possible when:

options.label: a
options.text: both metals share the same crystal structure

options.label: b
options.text: their atomic radii differ by more than 15%

options.label: c
options.text: they have a very strong chemical affinity

questions.keyExplanation: Complete solubility requires the same crystal structure.
questions.concise: Complete (total) solid solubility requires the same crystal structure.
questions.detailed:
Rule 1 states that **complete** solid solubility across the whole composition range
is only possible when both metals have the *same crystal structure*. This is why Cu–Ni
(both FCC) is fully isomorphous, while Fe–Cr and many others are not.
- (b) is the opposite — a size difference *above* 15% *restricts* solubility.
- (c) a strong chemical affinity *restricts* solubility (rule 3).
- (d) a large valence difference *reduces* solubility (rule 4).
Items (b), (c), (d) each state the *limiting* direction of the rule, not the condition for
complete solubility.

questions.text: Solid solubility is favoured when the atomic radii of the two metals differ by less than about:
questions.keyExplanation: ≈15% size misfit limit.
questions.concise: Size difference must be below ~15% for good solid solubility.
questions.detailed:
The relative size factor: solid solubility is favoured when the atomic radii of the
two metals differ by **less than about 15%**. Beyond that, the lattice strain restricts how much
solute the solvent can accommodate.
- (a) 3% is far too strict.
- (b) 8% is not the standard figure.
- (d) 30% is far too lenient.
Note the link to Ch. 7: this strain limit is exactly the solid-solution strengthening mechanism
pushed to its solubility limit.

questions.assertion: A strong chemical affinity between two metals tends to *restrict* their mutual solid solubility.
questions.reason: The atoms would rather bond into an ordered intermediate compound than stay randomly mixed in solution.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — strong affinity drives ordered compound formation instead of random solution.
questions.concise: Strong affinity drives the atoms to form an ordered compound rather than a random solution.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: a strong chemical affinity between two metals tends to *restrict* their mutual solid solubility.
- R is TRUE: the atoms would rather bond into an ordered intermediate compound than remain
  randomly mixed in solution.

R correctly explains A. The competing outcome is an *intermetallic compound* (Q12) — strong
affinity pulls the system toward a distinct ordered phase instead of a single disordered solid
solution. This is why many promising alloy pairs fail to give complete solubility.

questions.text: Cu–Ni is the standard isomorphous (complete-solid-solubility) teaching example because it satisfies all four Hume-Rothery rules. Which set of reasons is correct?

statements.text: same FCC crystal structure
less than 3% size difference
weak chemical affinity
similar valence

options.label: d
options.text:
1, 2 and 4 only

---

## Topic 4.3 — Intermediate alloy phases (Q11–Q15)

questions.keyExplanation: Cu–Ni satisfies all four rules.
questions.concise: Cu–Ni satisfies all four Hume-Rothery rules — hence complete isomorphous solubility.
questions.detailed:
Cu–Ni is the standard isomorphous teaching example because it satisfies **all four**
rules:
- Item 1 — same FCC crystal structure ✓
- Item 2 — less than 3% size difference ✓
- Item 3 — weak chemical affinity ✓
- Item 4 — similar valence ✓

Because all four are satisfied, Cu–Ni shows complete solid solubility across the entire
composition range — the textbook case of an isomorphous phase diagram.

questions.text: Match the intermediate-phase type to its example.
questions.keyExplanation: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Memorise this table — it is a classic match-the-following set.
questions.concise: valency compound = Mg₂Pb/Mg₂Sn/CaSe · interstitial = Fe₃C · e/a 3:2 BCC β = AgCd/Cu₂Al/FeAl · e/a 7:4 HCP ε = AgCd₃/Cu₃Si/FeZn₇.
questions.detailed:
| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| **Intermetallic (valency) compound** | Mg₂Pb, Mg₂Sn, CaSe — between chemically dissimilar metals, following ordinary valence rules |
| **Interstitial compound** | Fe₃C (cementite) — transition metal + small non-metal (H, C, N, B) |
| **Electron compound, e/a = 3:2, BCC β** | AgCd, Cu₂Al, FeAl |
| **Electron compound, e/a = 7:4, HCP ε** | AgCd₃, Cu₃Si, FeZn₇ |

This matching set is a classic exam item — the three electron-compound ratios (3:2 → BCC β,
21:13 → complex cubic γ, 7:4 → HCP ε) are worth memorising as a block.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *intermetallic (valency) compounds* is/are correct?

statements.text: They form between chemically dissimilar metals following ordinary rules of chemical valence.
Their properties are essentially non-metallic — hard and brittle.
They retain genuinely metallic character.
Examples include Mg₂Pb and Mg₂Sn.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 4 correct. Item 3 describes *interstitial* compounds, not valency compounds. [P2]
questions.concise: Valency compounds are non-metallic, hard and brittle; *interstitial* compounds retain metallic character.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: they form between chemically dissimilar metals following ordinary rules of
  chemical valence (e.g. CaSe, Mg₂Pb, Mg₂Sn).
- Item 2 — TRUE: their properties are essentially **non-metallic** — hard and brittle.
- Item 3 — FALSE: this describes **interstitial** compounds (Q13), not valency compounds. The
  metallic/non-metallic split is exactly the [P2] distinction between the two types.
- Item 4 — TRUE: Mg₂Pb and Mg₂Sn are standard examples.
Item 3 is a cross-contamination from the sibling category — the classic P1/P2 mechanism leaking
across.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *interstitial compounds* is/are correct?

statements.text: They form between a transition metal and a small non-metal (H, C, N, B).
Unlike valency compounds, they retain genuinely metallic character.
Fe₃C (cementite) is the most important example to a metallurgist.
They are always non-metallic and insulating.

questions.keyExplanation: Item 4 is false — interstitial compounds **retain metallic character** (that is the distinction from valency compounds).
questions.concise: Interstitial compounds = transition metal + small non-metal, retain metallic character, Fe₃C is the key example.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: they form between a transition metal and a small non-metal (H, C, N, B).
- Item 2 — TRUE: unlike valency compounds, they **retain genuinely metallic character**.
- Item 3 — TRUE: Fe₃C (cementite) is the most important example to a metallurgist.
- Item 4 — FALSE: this contradicts item 2. Interstitial compounds are *not* always non-metallic
  and insulating — that is the valency compounds' behaviour.
Item 4 is the false member. The metallic/non-metallic contrast is the sharpest way to separate
the two compound types:
| | character |
|---|---|
| Valency (intermetallic) | non-metallic, hard, brittle |
| Interstitial | retains metallic character |

questions.text: *Electron compounds* form at specific ratios of valence electrons to atoms. The 3:2 (21/13, 7/4) series corresponds to which structures?
questions.keyExplanation: 3:2 → BCC β; 21:13 → complex cubic γ; 7:4 → HCP ε.
questions.concise: e/a 3:2 = BCC β · 21:13 = complex cubic γ · 7:4 = HCP ε.
questions.detailed:
Electron compounds form at characteristic valence-electron-to-atom ratios, each with
a characteristic structure:
```
e/a = 3:2  → BCC            (β phase)    e.g. AgCd, Cu₂Al, FeAl
e/a = 21:13→ complex cubic  (γ phase)    e.g. Ag₂Cd₃, Cu₉Al₄, Fe₅Zn₂₁
e/a = 7:4  → HCP            (ε phase)    e.g. AgCd₃, Cu₃Si, FeZn₇
```
- (b), (c), (d) all shuffle the ratios to the wrong structures.
Memorise the sequence 3:2 → 21:13 → 7:4 mapping to BCC → complex cubic → HCP.

questions.text: Electron compounds are notable because they form at specific e/a ratios:

statements.text: largely independent of which particular elements are involved
and correspond to characteristic crystal structures
and only occur in copper-based alloys
and require identical atomic radii

options.label: d
options.text:
1, 2, 3 and 4

---

## Topic 4.4 — Tie-line and lever rules (Q16–Q25) **[HIGHEST-YIELD TOPIC]**

questions.keyExplanation: e/a ratios are essentially element-independent (1) and structure-specific (2). Items 3 and 4 are false.
questions.concise: e/a ratios are largely element-independent and structure-specific; not limited to Cu alloys, and no identical-radii requirement.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: they form at specific e/a ratios largely independent of which particular
  elements are involved.
- Item 2 — TRUE: and correspond to characteristic crystal structures.
- Item 3 — FALSE: they are not confined to copper-based alloys (though Cu systems are the
  classic examples — FeZn₇, for instance, is iron-zinc).
- Item 4 — FALSE: they do **not** require identical atomic radii.
Items 1 and 2 are the defining features; items 3 and 4 are unnecessary restrictions. The
electron-count rule is remarkably general — that is what makes it a "rule" worth naming.

questions.text: Inside the two-phase (L + α) region, at a given temperature, a horizontal tie line is drawn. Its intersection with the **liquidus** gives:

options.label: a
options.text: the composition of the liquid, C_L

options.label: b
options.text: the composition of the solid, C_S

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Liquidus → **liquid** composition C_L.
questions.concise: Liquidus intersection = **liquid** composition C_L. **This is your Quiz I Q5.**
questions.detailed:
**This is the exact question you lost in Quiz I.** Inside the two-phase (L + α)
region, a horizontal tie line is drawn at the temperature of interest. Its intersections give:
```
intersection with the LIQUIDUS  →  C_L  (composition of the LIQUID)
intersection with the SOLIDUS    →  C_S  (composition of the SOLID)
```
- (b) C_S comes from the *solidus*, not the liquidus.
- (c) the nominal composition C₀ is read off the *x-axis*, not from a tie-line intercept.
- (d) the invariant reaction temperature is horizontal on the diagram, unrelated to this.

**The mnemonic that stops this recurring:** *liquidus touches the liquid region; solidus touches
the solid region.* Say it once: **liquidus→liquid, solidus→solid**. You already had the mirror
of this question correct in the same quiz, so this is pure discrimination-under-distractors, not
a knowledge gap.

questions.text: The tie line's intersection with the **solidus** gives:
questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Solidus → **solid** composition C_S. Say it once: liquidus is the upper curve, solidus the lower, mushy between.
questions.concise: Solidus intersection = **solid** composition C_S.
questions.detailed:
The mirror of Q16. The tie line's intersection with the **solidus** gives the
composition of the **solid α** phase, C_S.
- (a) the liquid composition C_L comes from the *liquidus* (Q16).
- (c) the *average* composition is the nominal C₀, read from the x-axis — and it is fixed; only
  the *amounts* of the two phases change as you move through the two-phase field.
- (d) the eutectoid composition is a specific fixed point, not a tie-line intersection.
Q16 and Q17 together are worth committing to memory as a single paired fact.

questions.text: The correct statement of the lever rule is:

options.label: a
options.text: each phase's weight fraction uses the **opposite** arm of the tie line — the arm that does *not* touch that phase's own composition

options.label: b
options.text: each phase's weight fraction uses the arm on the **same** side as that phase

options.label: c
options.text: the lever arm is always taken from the liquidus only

options.label: d
options.text: the lever rule applies only at invariant points

questions.keyExplanation: Opposite arm — the arm not touching that phase's own composition.
questions.concise: Always the opposite arm. This is the single most error-prone rule in the chapter.
questions.detailed:
The lever rule assigns each phase the fraction given by the **opposite** arm:
```
W_L   = (C_S − C₀) / (C_S − C_L)     ← uses the arm from C₀ to C_S (the SOLID side)
W_α   = (C₀ − C_L) / (C_S − C_L)     ← uses the arm from C₀ to C_L (the LIQUID side)
```
The fraction of *liquid* is set by the arm reaching toward the *solid* composition, and vice versa.
- (b) using the same-side arm gives the *complement* (1 − W) — the classic error.
- (c), (d) are not the rule at all.
The physical intuition: if C₀ sits almost on the solidus, there is very little liquid — so the
liquid fraction must be small, which only the *solid-side* arm (a short arm) can give.

questions.text: The lever rule for the liquid fraction is:
questions.keyExplanation: W_L = (C_S − C₀)/(C_S − C_L).
questions.concise: W_L = (C_S − C₀)/(C_S − C_L).
questions.detailed:
```
W_L = (C_S − C₀) / (C_S − C_L)
```
The numerator is the arm from C₀ to C_S (the **opposite** side, Q18); the denominator is the
full tie-line length. Both arms always sum to 1: W_L + W_α = 1.
- (b) is the W_α formula.
- (c), (d) are not valid lever-rule forms.

questions.text: The lever rule for the solid fraction is:
questions.keyExplanation: W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_S − C_L).
questions.concise: W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_S − C_L).
questions.detailed:
```
W_α = (C₀ − C_L) / (C_S − C_L)
```
Numerator = the arm from C_L to C₀ (the **liquid** side — the opposite arm for the solid phase).
- (a) is the W_L formula.
- (c), (d) are invalid forms.
Note: **never** write W_α = (C_S − C₀)/(C_S − C_L) — that is W_L (Q19). Swapping the numerator
is the single most common lever-rule mistake.

questions.text: An alloy of C₀ = 50 wt% Ni is at a temperature where the tie line gives C_L = 30 wt% Ni and C_S = 55 wt% Ni. The weight fractions of liquid and solid are:
questions.detailed:
Given C₀ = 50, C_L = 30, C_S = 55:
```
tie-line length  = C_S − C_L = 55 − 30 = 25

W_L = (C_S − C₀)/(C_S − C_L) = (55 − 50)/25 = 5/25  = 0.20
W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_S − C_L) = (50 − 30)/25 = 20/25 = 0.80

check:  0.20 + 0.80 = 1.00  ✓
```
- (b) has the two fractions swapped (used the same-side arm, Q18).
- (c) 50/50 would only happen if C₀ were exactly midway.
- (d) 0.40/0.60 does not satisfy the lever rule for these values.
C₀ = 50 sits much closer to C_S = 55 than to C_L = 30, so the solid must dominate — 0.80 α.
That quick sanity check (which side is C₀ nearer?) catches most lever-rule slips instantly.

questions.assertion: In the worked lever-rule example (C₀ = 50, C_L = 30, C_S = 55), the majority phase is α at 80%.
questions.reason: C₀ = 50 sits much closer to C_S = 55 than to C_L = 30, and the majority phase is always the one whose composition C₀ is nearer.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — the majority phase is the one C₀ sits nearer.
questions.concise: C₀ nearer C_S ⇒ majority phase is α; the majority phase is always the one C₀ sits closer to.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: in the worked example the majority phase is α at 80%.
- R is TRUE: C₀ = 50 sits much closer to C_S = 55 than to C_L = 30, and the majority phase is
  always the one whose composition C₀ is nearer.

R correctly explains A. This is the qualitative check that should accompany every numerical
lever-rule calculation — if your answer says the majority phase is the one C₀ is far from,
you have used the wrong arm.

questions.text: At 1300 °C the Cu–Ni tie line meets the liquidus at 46% Ni and the solidus at 58% Ni. For a nominal alloy, the compositions of the two coexisting phases are:

options.label: c
options.text: both equal to the nominal composition

questions.keyExplanation: Liquidus intersection = C_L = 46% Ni; solidus intersection = C_S = 58% Ni. Neither equals the nominal composition.
questions.concise: Liquidus intersection = C_L = 46% Ni; solidus intersection = C_S = 58% Ni.
questions.detailed:
At 1300 °C the tie line meets:
```
the LIQUIDUS at 46% Ni  →  C_L = 46% Ni
the SOLIDUS at 58% Ni  →  C_S = 58% Ni
```
- (b) swaps the two.
- (c) the phase compositions are **never** equal to the nominal composition — that is the whole
  reason segregation exists (see Q24).
- (d) 50/54 is not what the tie line gives.
This is a direct application of Q16 and Q17 — liquidus→liquid, solidus→solid.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true of the tie-line rule?

statements.text: A horizontal line is drawn at the temperature of interest.
The liquidus intercept gives the liquid composition.
The solidus intercept gives the solid composition.
Both phase compositions always equal the nominal alloy composition.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the classic [P1] trap — the whole reason segregation exists is that the phase compositions differ from C₀.
questions.concise: A horizontal tie line at the temperature gives C_L from the liquidus and C_S from the solidus — they are *never* both equal to C₀.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: a horizontal line is drawn at the temperature of interest.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the liquidus intercept gives the liquid composition.
- Item 3 — TRUE: the solidus intercept gives the solid composition.
- Item 4 — FALSE: the two phase compositions are **never** equal to the nominal alloy
  composition C₀. If they were, there would be no segregation and no two-phase field.
Item 4 is the [P1] trap — an apparently-sensible statement that would render the entire tie-line
method pointless. The tie line's whole purpose is to show that the two coexisting phases have
*different* compositions.

questions.text: C₀ sitting close to C_S means:

statements.text: a short arm on the solid side
therefore a small numerator for W_L
therefore a small liquid fraction
therefore equal amounts of both phases

options.label: d
options.text:
1 and 4 only

---

## Topic 4.5 — Equilibrium solidification of an alloy (Q26–Q28)

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false.
questions.concise: C₀ near C_S ⇒ short solid-side arm ⇒ small numerator for W_L ⇒ small liquid fraction.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: C₀ sitting close to C_S gives a short arm on the solid side.
- Item 2 — TRUE: that short arm is the numerator for W_L (Q19).
- Item 3 — TRUE: therefore a small liquid fraction.
- Item 4 — FALSE: equal amounts would require C₀ to be exactly midway between C_L and C_S.
This traces the full logic chain, which is the reasoning behind Q21 and Q22. If you can follow
these four steps, you can reason about any lever-rule question without a calculator.

questions.text: During equilibrium solidification of an isomorphous alloy, freezing starts at T₁ where the C₀ vertical meets the liquidus. The very first solid to form has composition C_S1, which is:

options.label: a
options.text: richer in the higher-melting-point component than the liquid it froze from

questions.keyExplanation: First solid is richer in the higher-melting component (Ni in Cu–Ni).
questions.concise: First solid is richer in the higher-melting component (Ni in Cu–Ni).
questions.detailed:
During equilibrium solidification of an isomorphous alloy, freezing begins at T₁ where
the C₀ vertical meets the liquidus. The very first solid to form has composition C_S1, read off
the solidus at T₁, and it is **richer in the higher-melting-point component** (Ni, in Cu–Ni).
- (b), (c) are the opposite or equal.
- (d) the first solid is *not* C₀ — it is enriched in the higher-melting component.
This is why the solidus lies to the Ni-rich side of the liquidus in an isomorphous diagram, and
it is the starting point for the lever-rule calculation at every temperature.

questions.text: Equilibrium solidification finishes at the temperature at which:

options.label: a
options.text: the solidus finally reaches C₀ — the last trace of liquid disappears and the bulk solid is uniformly C₀

questions.keyExplanation: Freezing ends where the solidus reaches C₀.
questions.concise: Freezing ends where the solidus reaches C₀.
questions.detailed:
On continued cooling, the solid composition tracks the solidus and the liquid tracks
the liquidus. Freezing is complete at the temperature where the **solidus finally reaches C₀** —
at that point the last trace of liquid vanishes and the whole solid has the nominal composition C₀.
- (b) is the *start* of freezing (liquidus meets C₀), not the end.
- (c), (d) are not the defining conditions.
**Note the caveat in Q28:** this uniform-C₀ end state requires *infinitely slow* cooling so that
solid-state diffusion can keep the solid homogeneous — which is exactly why real castings core
(§4.7).

questions.assertion: For the solid's composition to track the solidus continuously during cooling, atoms already inside the solid must keep rearranging by diffusion.
questions.reason: This is only physically realistic at infinitely slow cooling — so it never happens in a real casting.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — and this is exactly why Section 4.7 (coring) exists.
questions.concise: Tracking the solidus requires solid-state diffusion — only realistic at infinitely slow cooling, so it never happens in a real casting.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: for the solid's composition to track the solidus continuously, atoms already inside
  the solid must keep rearranging by diffusion.
- R is TRUE: this is only physically realistic at infinitely slow cooling — so it never happens
  in a real casting.

R correctly explains A, and it is the bridge to the whole of §4.7. Because real cooling is too
fast for solid-state diffusion, the growing solid cannot stay homogeneous, so the average solid
composition lags the equilibrium solidus — producing **coring** (Q32–Q35). The equilibrium
solidification of Q26–Q27 is therefore a limiting case, not a description of reality.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *constitutional supercooling* is/are correct?

statements.text: As the interface advances it rejects solute faster than that solute can diffuse away, building a solute-enriched boundary layer.
The local liquidus temperature ahead of the interface depends on that local composition.
Whenever the actual temperature profile rises more slowly near the interface than the local liquidus does, a zone of constitutionally supercooled liquid opens up.
It is driven by temperature rather than composition.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false — it is driven by **composition**, not temperature. [P2]
questions.concise: Solute pile-up raises the local liquidus faster than the actual T falls → supercooled zone → planar front breaks down. It is composition-driven, not temperature-driven.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: as the interface advances it rejects solute faster than that solute can diffuse
  away, building a solute-enriched boundary layer.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the local liquidus temperature ahead of the interface depends on that local composition.
- Item 3 — TRUE: whenever the actual temperature profile rises more slowly near the interface
  than the local liquidus does, a zone of constitutionally supercooled liquid opens up.
- Item 4 — FALSE: it is driven by **composition**, not temperature. The name *constitutional*
  means *composition-related* — this is the [P2] discriminator from plain thermal undercooling.
The [P2] rule: *thermal undercooling = temperature-driven (pure metal); constitutional
supercooling = composition-driven (alloy).*

questions.assertion: Constitutional supercooling is the dominant reason alloy ingots develop a pronounced central equiaxed zone.
questions.reason: As the columnar front advances, the thermal gradient shallows and the constitutionally supercooled zone widens until new grains nucleate within the supercooled liquid ahead of the front — the columnar-to-equiaxed transition.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — this is the columnar-to-equiaxed transition mechanism.
questions.concise: As the columnar front advances the gradient shallows and the supercooled zone widens until new grains nucleate ahead — the columnar-to-equiaxed transition.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: constitutional supercooling is the dominant reason alloy ingots develop a pronounced
  central equiaxed zone.
- R is TRUE: as the columnar front advances, the thermal gradient shallows and the constitutionally
  supercooled zone widens until new grains nucleate *within* the supercooled liquid ahead of the
  front — this is the **columnar-to-equiaxed transition**.

R correctly explains A. It ties Ch. 3's ingot structure (Q29) to Ch. 4's alloy-solidification
mechanism, which is exactly the kind of cross-chapter link examiners favour.

questions.text: A planar interface cannot survive constitutional supercooling because:

options.label: a
options.text: any protrusion poking into the supercooled zone finds extra undercooling driving it forward, breaking the front down into cells and then dendrites

options.label: d
options.text:
surface tension is overcome

---

## Topic 4.7 — Non-equilibrium solidification and coring (Q32–Q37)

questions.keyExplanation: Protrusion into the supercooled zone → preferential growth → cells → dendrites.
questions.concise: A protrusion into the supercooled zone wins the growth race → cells → dendrites.
questions.detailed:
A planar interface cannot survive constitutional supercooling because any protrusion
that pokes into the constitutionally supercooled zone finds *extra undercooling* driving it
forward, so it grows faster than the surrounding front. Repeated amplification breaks the planar
front down first into **cells**, then into **dendrites**.
- (b), (c), (d) are not the mechanism.
This is the alloy analogue of Q23 (thermal instability in pure metals) — same "bump wins"
instability, different driving field.

questions.text: *Coring* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a composition gradient within a cast grain — from a high-melting core to a low-melting, solute-rich edge

options.label: b
options.text: a crack along the grain boundary

options.label: d
options.text: an oxide film on the grain surface

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Coring = composition gradient *within a grain*.
questions.concise: Coring = composition gradient *within* one grain (high-melting core → low-melting edge).
questions.detailed:
**Coring** is a composition gradient *within* a cast grain: the grain has a
high-melting (solute-lean) core that froze first, and a low-melting, solute-rich edge that froze
last.
- (b) describes a crack, not a composition gradient.
- (c) a blowhole is gas porosity.
- (d) an oxide film is a surface defect.
The [P2] discriminator: **coring is grain-scale (microsegregation)**, contrasted with the
ingot-scale normal/inverse/gravity segregation of Ch. 3 Q48. Different length scale, different name.

questions.text: Coring occurs because:

statements.text: real cooling is too fast for solid-state diffusion to keep the growing solid homogeneous
the average solid composition consistently lags behind the equilibrium solidus
a shallower effective (non-equilibrium) solidus is traced out
solid-state diffusion is infinitely fast in real castings

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 states the exact opposite of the mechanism.
questions.concise: Real cooling is too fast for solid-state diffusion, so the average solid composition lags the equilibrium solidus and a shallower effective solidus is traced.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: real cooling is too fast for solid-state diffusion to keep the growing solid homogeneous.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the average solid composition consistently lags behind the equilibrium solidus.
- Item 3 — TRUE: a shallower effective (non-equilibrium) solidus is therefore traced out.
- Item 4 — FALSE: this states the exact *opposite* of item 1. Solid-state diffusion is infinitely
  slow in real castings relative to the cooling rate — that is precisely the problem.
Items 1 and 4 are direct opposites, so item 4 is the false member that defeats an "all" option.

questions.text: Under non-equilibrium cooling, freezing actually finishes at T₄ which is:

options.label: a
options.text: lower than the equilibrium finish temperature T₃

questions.keyExplanation: T₄ < T₃ — the effective solidus lags below the equilibrium solidus.
questions.concise: Under non-equilibrium cooling, freezing finishes at T₄ < T₃.
questions.detailed:
Because the average solid composition lags the equilibrium solidus (Q33), the
effective solidus sits *below* the equilibrium one, and freezing actually finishes at **T₄ which
is lower than T₃**.
- (b), (c), (d) all contradict this.
The practical consequence (Q38–Q41): the *effective* solidus, not the equilibrium solidus, is
what governs local melting — so a cored alloy can start melting at a temperature that looks safe
on the equilibrium diagram.

questions.text: In a cored grain, the composition varies from:

options.label: a
options.text: a high-melting (solute-rich) core, frozen first, to a low-melting (solute-lean) edge at the grain boundary, frozen last

options.label: b
options.text: a solute-lean core to a solute-rich edge

options.label: d
options.text: a carbon-rich edge to a carbon-free core

questions.keyExplanation: High-melting core (frozen first) → low-melting edge at the grain boundary (frozen last).
questions.concise: High-melting core (frozen first) → low-melting edge at the grain boundary (frozen last).
questions.detailed:
Within a cored grain the composition varies from a **high-melting core** (frozen
first) to a **low-melting edge** at the grain boundary (frozen last). In Cu–Ni terms: a Ni-rich
core, Ni-lean edge.
- (b), (c), (d) are either the reverse or uniform.
**Note on the wording in this option:** it says "high-melting (solute-rich) core". The essential
physics is *high-melting first-frozen core → low-melting last-frozen edge*. In Cu–Ni the core is
Ni-rich (Ni being the higher-melting component), so the core is high-melting. The last-frozen
edge is enriched in the *lower*-melting component, which is the part that can melt first on
reheating — the origin of burning (Q38).

questions.text: In peritectic systems, the analogous pattern to coring is called *surrounding (enveloping)* because:

options.label: a
options.text: the peritectic reaction L + β → α produces a shell of α that envelops the untransformed β core, insulating it and starving the reaction of contact area

options.label: c
options.text: the α phase is entirely consumed

options.label: d
options.text: a eutectic forms at the boundary

questions.keyExplanation: L + β → α shell enveloping and insulating the unreacted β core.
questions.concise: Peritectic: α shell envelops the β core, insulating it and starving the reaction.
questions.detailed:
In peritectic systems, the reaction **L + β → α** occurs at the interface between
the liquid and the solid β. The α product forms as a **shell around the β core**, which:
- **insulates** the untransformed β from the liquid, and
- **starves the reaction** of further contact area.

Because the reaction needs contact between L and β, and the α shell physically separates them,
the transformation cannot proceed to completion — a classic non-equilibrium defect.
- (b), (c), (d) describe other outcomes, not the peritectic enveloping mechanism.

questions.text: Non-equilibrium solidification, compared with the equilibrium prediction:

statements.text: lowers the effective freezing temperature
widens the apparent freezing range
leaves the last liquid enriched in low-melting solute at grain boundaries
has no effect on the phase diagram interpretation

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 false.
questions.concise: Non-equilibrium cooling lowers the effective freezing temperature, widens the freezing range, and enriches the last liquid at grain boundaries.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it lowers the effective freezing temperature (T₄ < T₃, Q34).
- Item 2 — TRUE: it widens the apparent freezing range.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it leaves the last liquid enriched in low-melting solute at grain boundaries —
  which is exactly where burning will occur on reheating (Q42).
- Item 4 — FALSE: it profoundly changes how you interpret the phase diagram — you must use the
  *effective* solidus, not the equilibrium one, to avoid burning.
Items 1–3 are the consequences; item 4 denies that any reinterpretation is needed, which is
the dangerous error that leads to burning.

questions.text: *Burning* during homogenisation or solution treatment is:

options.label: a
options.text: genuine grain-boundary melting (liquation) caused by crossing the local effective solidus — permanent, unrecoverable damage

options.label: b
options.text: simple loss of ductility recoverable by re-annealing

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Burning = crossing the *effective* solidus → grain-boundary melting → permanent.
questions.concise: Burning = crossing the effective (cored) solidus → grain-boundary melting → permanent.
questions.detailed:
**Burning** (burning-up / liquation) is *genuine grain-boundary melting* caused by
crossing the local **effective** (cored) solidus. Once the grain boundaries have melted:
- the material is permanently damaged — it cannot be recovered by any subsequent heat treatment;
- on cooling the boundaries are oxidised and embrittled, often with microcracking.

- (b) describes **overheating** (Q39), which *is* recoverable.
- (c) surface oxidation is a different, superficial defect.
- (d) it is damaging, not beneficial.
The [P2] test: *did it cross the effective solidus and actually melt?* If yes → burning (permanent).

questions.text: *Overheating* is:

options.label: a
options.text: heating close to, but not across, the local solidus — driving segregation and grain-boundary precipitation with loss of ductility, but recoverable by proper subsequent heat treatment

options.label: b
options.text: grain-boundary melting that permanently ruins the material

options.label: d
options.text: quenching from too high a temperature

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Overheating = approaching but not crossing → recoverable.
questions.concise: Overheating = approaching but not crossing the solidus → recoverable.
questions.detailed:
**Overheating** is heating *close to* — but **not across** — the local solidus. The
effects are:
- accelerated segregation and grain-boundary precipitation,
- a loss of ductility and toughness,
but crucially **no melting**, so the condition is **recoverable** by a proper subsequent heat
treatment (e.g. re-solution-treat + quench, or a re-anneal).
- (b), (c) describe **burning**, not overheating.
- (d) quenching from too high a temperature is a different matter (and can cause burning if it
  crosses the solidus).
**Q38 vs Q39 is the single most important paired distinction in Chapter 4:**
| | Overheating | Burning |
|---|---|---|
| Crosses the effective solidus? | No | **Yes** |
| Melting? | No | **Yes** (grain boundary) |
| Recoverable? | **Yes** | No — permanent |

questions.assertion: Burning is permanent, unrecoverable material damage, whereas overheating can be recovered by proper subsequent heat treatment.
questions.reason: The difference is whether the anneal actually crossed the *effective* (cored) solidus at the grain boundaries, causing genuine melting.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — the distinction is whether melting occurred.
questions.concise: The difference is whether the anneal crossed the effective (cored) solidus and caused melting.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: burning is permanent, unrecoverable damage, whereas overheating can be recovered by
  proper subsequent heat treatment.
- R is TRUE: the difference is whether the anneal actually crossed the *effective* (cored) solidus
  at the grain boundaries, causing genuine melting.

R correctly explains A. The entire distinction rests on one question — *was there melting?* —
and that in turn rests on comparing your temperature to the **effective**, not the equilibrium,
solidus. This is the highest-value concept in Chapter 4.

questions.text: The practical rule that follows is:

statements.text: a cored, as-cast structure must never be homogenised or solution-treated right up against its equilibrium solidus temperature
because the effective solidus at the grain boundaries sits *below* the equilibrium one
homogenisation should start well below the equilibrium solidus and be raised only as coring is removed
the equilibrium solidus is the correct temperature to target

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the dangerous error that causes burning.
questions.concise: Never treat a cored alloy up against its equilibrium solidus, because the effective solidus at grain boundaries sits below it; start well below and raise only as coring is removed.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: a cored, as-cast structure must never be homogenised or solution-treated right
  up against its equilibrium solidus temperature.
- Item 2 — TRUE: because the effective solidus at the grain boundaries sits *below* the equilibrium one.
- Item 3 — TRUE: homogenisation should start well below the equilibrium solidus and be raised
  only as coring is removed (as the composition becomes uniform, the effective solidus rises
  toward the equilibrium one).
- Item 4 — FALSE: targeting the equilibrium solidus is precisely the error that causes burning.
Item 4 is the dangerous false member. The safe practice is to work from the *effective* solidus
upward, never to aim at the equilibrium line.

questions.text: Coring concentrates the lowest-melting material precisely:

options.label: a
options.text: at grain boundaries and interdendritic spaces, where it can begin to melt at a temperature that looks safe on the equilibrium diagram

options.label: d
options.text:
in the centre of primary dendrite arms

---
---

questions.keyExplanation: Low-melting material concentrates at boundaries/interdendritic spaces.
questions.concise: Low-melting material concentrates at boundaries/interdendritic spaces — the first place to melt on reheating.
questions.detailed:
Coring concentrates the lowest-melting material precisely at **grain boundaries and
interdendritic spaces** — the last regions to solidify (Q35). On reheating, these are therefore
the *first* regions to melt, at a temperature that looks entirely safe if you consult only the
**equilibrium** diagram.
- (b), (c), (d) all place the low-melting material somewhere other than the boundaries.
This is the direct mechanism of burning (Q38), and it is why the effective-solidus rule of Q41
exists. Chain it together: **coring → solute at boundaries → low local solidus → burn on reheating**.
